ashoka.title: Ashoka: a life in 60 moments
ashoka.introHtml: Follow Ashoka from a royal childhood known mostly through later stories to the conquests, journeys, and reforms recorded in his own inscriptions. Dates are approximate where marked; many events are securely dated only by years after his consecration. His conventional reign is c. 268–232 BCE. [1–3, 7]

chapters.title: A prince whose birthplace is uncertain
chapters.html: Ashoka was born into the Mauryan royal family, traditionally around 304 BCE. His father was Bindusara and his grandfather was Chandragupta Maurya. No surviving contemporary record securely identifies his birthplace. Pataliputra was his dynasty’s capital, but that does not prove that he was born there. [1, 2, 7]

chapters.title: The stories about his mother
chapters.html: Later Buddhist traditions give Ashoka’s mother different identities. A northern account calls her Subhadrangi, a Brahmin’s daughter from Champa who entered Bindusara’s household. This is a story preserved long after his lifetime. Champa is her home in that narrative; it does not establish her son’s birthplace. [2, 7]

chapters.title: An empire built before him
chapters.html: His grandfather Chandragupta had founded the Mauryan dynasty after the fall of the Nandas. His father inherited its power, and Ashoka would become its third emperor. He therefore grew up within an established monarchy, with armies, provincial governors, rival royal relatives, and obligations that reached far beyond the palace. [1, 2, 7]

articles.title: Born from Poison: The Chilling Legend Behind Bindusara’s Name

chapters.date: Before and during his reign · Pataliputra
chapters.title: Pataliputra at the centre
chapters.html: The dynasty’s capital stood near modern Patna, connected to the river routes of the Gangetic plain. This was the political centre from which a distant province had to be reached by messengers, officials, and armies. Ashoka’s later concern with reports and inspections makes sense against that problem of distance. [1]

chapters.title: A prince remembered at Taxila
chapters.html: Northern Buddhist stories send the young Ashoka to Taxila, in the northwest, during unrest. They portray the people as angry with officials rather than with the king or prince. The episode introduces him as a provincial problem-solver, but it is later testimony rather than a surviving report from his youth. [7]

chapters.date: Before his accession · Ujjain and Vidisha
chapters.title: A posting in central India
chapters.html: The Mahavamsa connects Ashoka’s early career with Ujjain, in Avanti. This places the remembered prince in central India before his accession. The association is important to his family story and later Buddhist connections, although it comes from a chronicle compiled centuries after the events it describes. [3]

chapters.title: Devi of Vidisha
chapters.html: In that chronicle, Ashoka meets Devi at Vidisha on his way to Ujjain. She becomes the mother of Mahinda and Sanghamitta, figures central to Sri Lankan Buddhist history. The account connects royal family life with a region near Sanchi; it should be read as the chronicle’s tradition, not contemporary marriage documentation. [3]

chapters.title: Two children with a larger legacy
chapters.html: The Sri Lankan chronicles identify Mahinda and Sanghamitta as Ashoka’s children and connect both with entry into the Buddhist order. Their later journeys give his family an importance beyond succession to the throne. Those relationships are preserved in Buddhist historical traditions rather than in Ashoka’s surviving family inscriptions. [3–5]

chapters.title: A disputed path to the throne
chapters.html: Ashoka’s accession is conventionally placed in the years before his consecration around 268 BCE. Later accounts describe violent rivalry among Bindusara’s sons, but their details differ. The familiar claim that he killed ninety-nine brothers is a chronicle’s claim; his own inscriptions still refer to brothers and other royal relatives. [1, 2, 7]

chapters.title: The reign becomes easier to follow
chapters.html: After consecration, Ashoka counted the years used in his inscriptions. These dates anchor a conquest in year eight, a journey in year ten, and later reforms. His common royal designation was Devanampriya Priyadarshi, often rendered “Beloved of the Gods, Piyadasi.” Some inscriptions also connect that designation with the personal name Ashoka. [1]

chapters.date: Early and middle reign · The Buddhist community
chapters.title: Becoming a Buddhist gradually
chapters.html: In Minor Rock Edict I, Ashoka says he had been a lay follower for more than two and a half years before becoming strongly committed after contact with the Sangha. His own account describes stages of religious effort. It does not securely support the familiar scene of an instantaneous conversion immediately after Kalinga. [1]

articles.title: Minor Rock Edict I: Ashoka’s effort

chapters.date: Early and middle reign · The Buddhist community
chapters.title: An emperor who admitted he had changed
chapters.html: Ashoka acknowledged that his early religious effort had been limited. He also urged people of low status to strive, making spiritual progress something beyond royal rank. His Buddhist commitment did not make him a monk: he remained an emperor, householder, and ruler responsible for administration and punishment. [1]

articles.title: Minor Rock Edict I: Ashoka’s effort

chapters.title: The invasion of Kalinga
chapters.html: In his eighth year after consecration, conventionally around 261 BCE, Ashoka conquered Kalinga, in eastern India around present-day Odisha. Major Rock Edict XIII is the central contemporary record. It describes the conquest’s human consequences, but does not give us a complete battle narrative or identify every leader who resisted him. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XIII: After the conquest of Kalinga

chapters.title: The terrible figures he recorded
chapters.html: Ashoka reported 150,000 people deported, 100,000 killed, and many times that number dead after the conquest. These are royal claims, not independently verified statistics. Their meaning is nevertheless unmistakable: the campaign involved killing, forced displacement, and suffering that extended beyond those directly slain in combat. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XIII: After the conquest of Kalinga

chapters.title: People torn from their lives
chapters.html: Deportation was part of the victory Ashoka described. His inscription does not tell us where every displaced person went or what became of them. Remembering those people matters: Kalinga was a disaster for conquered communities before it became the famous turning point in an emperor’s life story. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XIII: After the conquest of Kalinga

chapters.date: After the conquest · Major Rock Edict XIII
chapters.title: Remorse enters the royal record
chapters.html: Ashoka’s remorse concerned more than soldiers. He described suffering among householders, religious people, relatives, friends, and dependants: injury to one person wounded others connected with them. The inscription preserves his later public judgment. It does not record an eyewitness scene of him walking through a battlefield of corpses. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XIII: After the conquest of Kalinga

chapters.date: After the conquest · Dhauli and Jaugada
chapters.title: He still had to govern Kalinga
chapters.html: Remorse did not reverse the annexation. In the Separate Rock Edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada, Ashoka instructed officials to avoid unjust imprisonment and harsh treatment. The conquered country now received commands about restraint in government. Whether every officer followed them is a question the surviving texts cannot answer. [1]

articles.title: Separate Rock Edict I: Justice in Kalinga
Separate Rock Edict II: Trust on the frontier

chapters.title: “All people are my children”
chapters.html: Ashoka described people as his children and wished for their welfare in this world and the next. This expressed care within a monarchy: he still expected authority and obedience. His officials were told to resist anger, jealousy, cruelty, and impatience, because those habits could turn royal administration into suffering. [1]

articles.title: Separate Rock Edict I: Justice in Kalinga
Separate Rock Edict II: Trust on the frontier

chapters.title: The power to punish remained
chapters.html: Even the edict expressing remorse over Kalinga warned forest peoples that the king retained the power to punish. Ashoka preferred victory through dhamma, but did not dissolve his government or renounce every threat of force. His concern for restraint and his coercive authority existed together. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XIII: After the conquest of Kalinga

chapters.title: A journey to the Buddha’s awakening place
chapters.html: In his tenth year after consecration, Ashoka went to Sambodhi, generally understood as Bodh Gaya. Major Rock Edict VIII contrasted this with royal pleasure tours. His preferred journey involved religious visits, gifts, meeting older people, and discussion of dhamma: a different public purpose for a king’s travels. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict VIII: Journeys for dhamma

chapters.date: From the twelfth regnal year · Across the empire
chapters.title: What he meant by dhamma
chapters.html: Ashoka’s public dhamma concerned right conduct: care for parents, generosity, truthfulness, restraint, and consideration for living beings. Some inscriptions explicitly express his Buddhism; many public edicts address a wider religious audience. His moral programme connected the emperor’s convictions with the daily relationships of households, workplaces, and communities. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict III: Five-year tours of instruction
Major Rock Edict XI: The gift of dhamma

chapters.title: Everyday conduct mattered
chapters.html: His teaching reached servants and enslaved people as well as parents, children, friends, and religious communities. He urged people to treat dependants properly and to value the gift of moral guidance. These instructions did not abolish social hierarchy or slavery; they challenged conduct within relationships that the monarchy continued to recognise. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XI: The gift of dhamma

chapters.title: Good conduct above ceremonies
chapters.html: Major Rock Edict IX criticised the value placed on ceremonies surrounding sickness, marriage, childbirth, and travel. Ashoka preferred a “ceremony of dhamma”: restraint, proper treatment of others, and respect for religious people. This was the king’s intervention in everyday customs, not proof that everyone abandoned their own practices. [1]

chapters.date: Twelfth year after consecration · The provinces
chapters.title: Officials took the message on tour
chapters.html: In his twelfth year, Ashoka ordered officials to make periodic tours combining ordinary duties with instruction in dhamma. His programme therefore depended on people who travelled, inspected, and spoke. It was not simply a collection of words on stone: the king wanted his instructions carried into provincial life. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict III: Five-year tours of instruction

chapters.date: Twelfth and nineteenth regnal years · Barabar
chapters.title: Caves given to the Ajivikas
chapters.html: At Barabar, inscriptions record cave dedications to the Ajivikas, including the Sudama cave in Ashoka’s twelfth year. These surviving records show patronage beyond Buddhism. The polished rock-cut chambers also remind us that religious gifts involved skilled labour and durable spaces, not only declarations of goodwill toward other communities. [1]

articles.title: Sudama Cave inscription: A gift to the Ajivikas
Karna Chaupar Cave inscription: Shelter for the rainy season

chapters.date: Thirteenth year after consecration · Across the empire
chapters.title: A new kind of royal officer
chapters.html: In his thirteenth year, Ashoka appointed dhamma-mahamatras. Their responsibilities included religious communities, vulnerable people, prisoners, and royal households. Major Rock Edict V presents this as a new institution. The emperor was trying to attach his moral programme to official duties rather than leaving it entirely to individual choice. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict V: Officers of dhamma

chapters.title: Reports were to reach him anywhere
chapters.html: Major Rock Edict VI says public business should be reported to Ashoka even while he was eating or in private surroundings. He presented government as a continuing obligation, not work confined to an audience hall. This records his ideal of accessibility; it cannot prove that every distant complaint reached him promptly. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict VI: Reports at every hour

chapters.date: The public edicts · The royal kitchen
chapters.title: Change began in his own kitchen
chapters.html: Major Rock Edict I describes a sharp reduction in animals killed for the royal kitchen and an intention to end the remaining killings. Ashoka also condemned certain sacrifices and gatherings. These measures did not amount to a documented ban on all meat eating throughout the empire; his regulations had specific limits. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict I: Animal sacrifice and the royal kitchen

chapters.title: Listen before condemning another faith
chapters.html: In Major Rock Edict XII, Ashoka urged restraint when praising one’s own religious community and criticising another. He wanted people to hear and understand other teachings. His support for Buddhism remained clear, but this public instruction asked for respect across the religious diversity of his empire. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XII: Restraint in religious speech

chapters.date: During his reign · The Bairat edict
chapters.title: His own Buddhist allegiance was explicit
chapters.html: The Bairat or Bhabru edict expresses Ashoka’s reverence for the Buddha, dhamma, and Sangha. It recommends Buddhist teachings for monks, nuns, and lay followers to hear and consider. His broader respect for communities therefore coexisted with personal religious commitment and an active interest in Buddhist learning. [1]

articles.title: Bairat Edict: Texts for the Buddhist community

chapters.title: He intervened inside the Sangha
chapters.html: Ashoka’s schism edicts demanded unity in the Buddhist community. A monk or nun responsible for division was to wear white clothing and live outside the monastic residence. Royal officials helped communicate and enforce these orders. Supporting a religious institution could also mean using government authority to discipline its members. [1]

articles.title: Schism Edict: Unity of the Saṃgha

chapters.date: Middle reign onward · Southern India and the northwest
chapters.title: Southern kingdoms were neighbours too
chapters.html: Ashoka’s inscriptions name the Cholas, Pandyas, Satyaputras, and Keralaputras in the world beyond or beside his dominions. The Mauryan Empire should not be drawn as identical with modern India. Direct administration, neighbouring kingdoms, frontier relations, and claims of moral influence were different things in his political geography. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XIII: After the conquest of Kalinga
Kandahar bilingual inscription: Piety and truth

chapters.title: Speaking to the northwest in its languages
chapters.html: At Kandahar, in present-day Afghanistan, a Greek-Aramaic inscription communicated Ashoka’s message to a multilingual region. A separate Greek text preserves material corresponding to Major Rock Edicts XII and XIII. These are distinct records, showing adaptation for audiences whose linguistic worlds differed from those of the Gangetic heartland. [8]

articles.title: Kandahar bilingual inscription: Piety and truth

chapters.title: He knew of distant Hellenistic rulers
chapters.html: Major Rock Edict XIII names rulers commonly identified with Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus Gonatas, Magas, and an Alexander whose identification is disputed. That Alexander is not Alexander the Great. Ashoka claimed far-reaching victory through dhamma; the inscription does not establish Mauryan military conquest of those kingdoms. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict XIII: After the conquest of Kalinga

chapters.date: Throughout his reign · The inscriptional landscape
chapters.title: A king who left his words in stone
chapters.html: Ashoka placed messages on rocks, pillars, and cave walls across a large territory. Many use Prakrit and Brahmi, while northwestern records include Kharoshthi, Greek, and Aramaic. His voice survives through this distributed record. Hearing inscriptions read aloud also mattered in a world where many people could not read them themselves. [1, 8]

articles.title: Ashoka’s edicts and inscriptions: a guide to the surviving texts

chapters.date: The Mauryan pillars · Their later history
chapters.title: Monuments with lives after his own
chapters.html: His pillars made royal messages durable, but their later histories changed their settings. The Topra pillar, for example, was moved to Delhi by Firuz Shah Tughlaq in the fourteenth century. Seeing it at Kotla today means encountering both Ashoka’s inscription and a monument reshaped by later rulers’ ambitions. [1, 11]

articles.title: How Ashoka's Pillar Came to Tughlaq's Delhi: Forty-Two Wheels, One Ancient Mystery

chapters.date: During his reign · The royal household
chapters.title: Karuvaki appears in a surviving order
chapters.html: The Queen’s Edict identifies Karuvaki, the second queen and mother of Tivara, and directs that her donations be recorded as hers. This is unusually direct evidence about a royal woman. It establishes her recognised giving and family connection, without supplying a full biography or proving every later story about Ashoka’s queens. [1]

articles.title: Queen’s Edict: Gifts of Karuvaki

chapters.title: The difficult stories about Kunala
chapters.html: Northern Buddhist tradition tells of Kunala, a prince blinded through a forged order amid palace intrigue. The account explores desire, suffering, and religious merit. It is important to Ashoka’s remembered family life, but it is not a contemporary case record from which every accusation against a queen can be treated as established. [7]

chapters.date: Fourteenth and twentieth years · Nepal Terai
chapters.title: Honouring an earlier Buddha
chapters.html: At Nigali Sagar, Ashoka’s inscription says that he enlarged the stupa of Kanakamuni Buddha in his fourteenth year and visited in his twentieth. The record reveals a sacred geography wider than places associated only with Gautama Buddha. Its regnal dates give us firmer anchors than later elaborate pilgrimage stories. [1]

articles.title: Nigali Sagar Pillar Edict: The Konakamana stupa

chapters.title: Another dated gift at Barabar
chapters.html: The Karna Chaupar cave inscription records a dedication in Ashoka’s nineteenth regnal year. Unlike some Barabar records, it does not explicitly name the Ajivikas in its surviving wording. The distinction matters: neighbouring monuments and a shared patron do not justify silently adding a recipient absent from a particular text. [1]

articles.title: Karna Chaupar Cave inscription: Shelter for the rainy season

chapters.title: At Lumbini, a visit written down
chapters.html: In his twentieth year, Ashoka visited Lumbini, identified by the inscription as the birthplace of the Buddha. The text records royal honour and a fiscal concession for the village. It documents a particular visit and place; it does not establish every stop on the longer pilgrimage itineraries in later literature. [1]

articles.title: Lumbini Pillar Edict: The Buddha’s birthplace

chapters.date: Later Buddhist tradition · Pataliputra to Anuradhapura
chapters.title: A council remembered at Pataliputra
chapters.html: Sri Lankan Buddhist tradition places a Third Council under Ashoka’s patronage at Pataliputra, associated with Moggaliputta Tissa. It connects the council with religious missions. These accounts matter deeply to Buddhist history, but Ashoka’s own edicts do not supply a matching contemporary narrative of the council’s proceedings. [2, 4]

chapters.title: Mahinda’s journey to Lanka
chapters.html: The Mahavamsa describes Mahinda travelling to Lanka and meeting Devanampiyatissa, its ruler. It connects the journey with the establishment of Buddhism there and with Ashoka’s family. The chronicle preserves this remembered relationship across the sea; its speeches and detailed scenes should not be mistaken for contemporary transcripts. [3, 4]

chapters.title: Sanghamitta and the women’s order
chapters.html: The chronicle gives Sanghamitta a vital role when women in Lanka seek ordination. She travels with a branch of the Bodhi tree and helps establish the nuns’ community. This story makes a royal daughter central to religious continuity, rather than treating the expansion of Buddhism as the work of male envoys alone. [5]

chapters.date: Mauryan patronage and later building · Sanchi
chapters.title: Sanchi grew through many generations
chapters.html: Sanchi preserves an important Mauryan association within a monument complex transformed by later patrons. Its famous sculptured gateways belong to later periods, not to Ashoka’s own lifetime. They show how Buddhist communities continued building and remembering; they should not be presented as eyewitness portraits or an unchanged scene from his reign. [3, 10]

chapters.title: Care for people and animals
chapters.html: Major Rock Edict II describes medical provision for humans and animals, and the obtaining and planting of medicinal plants, roots, and fruits where lacking. This places material welfare within the ruler’s declared responsibilities. It does not establish a modern public-health system or prove that every settlement had a staffed hospital. [1]

articles.title: Major Rock Edict II: Care for people and animals

chapters.title: Shade, wells, and places to rest
chapters.html: In his late summary, Ashoka describes banyan trees for shade, mango groves, wells, watering places, and rest facilities along routes. These works served moving people and animals. He also acknowledged earlier kings’ welfare efforts: his significance does not depend on pretending that nobody before him had planted a tree or dug a well. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict VII: A royal review of dhamma

chapters.date: Twenty-sixth year after consecration · District administration
chapters.title: Justice remained a duty of government
chapters.html: In his twenty-sixth year, Ashoka’s Pillar Edict IV entrusted rajukas with discretion over rewards and penalties while calling for consistency in justice. His officers were to act confidently and responsibly. This was a reform within monarchical government, not the creation of a modern independent judiciary or the abolition of punishment. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict IV: Justice and the rajukas

chapters.title: Three days before execution
chapters.html: The same edict granted a three-day reprieve to people condemned to death, allowing relatives to appeal or the condemned to prepare religiously. The measure matters precisely because execution remained possible. Ashoka’s concern for restraint should not be rewritten as a claim that he abolished capital punishment throughout his empire. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict IV: Justice and the rajukas

chapters.title: Repeated releases of prisoners
chapters.html: Pillar Edict V says that prisoners had been released on twenty-five occasions by the twenty-sixth year. The text does not identify every person, offence, or condition. It records repeated royal acts of release, but cannot support the stronger claim that every prison was emptied or all sentences were cancelled each year. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict V: Protection of animals

chapters.title: Detailed rules for living creatures
chapters.html: In Pillar Edict V, Ashoka listed protected creatures and restricted practices including certain killings, forest burning, and treatment of working animals. Some ancient species names remain uncertain. The rules show an effort to reduce injury within existing life and livelihoods, rather than a documented end to all human use of animals. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict V: Protection of animals

chapters.title: Look for faults in yourself
chapters.html: Pillar Edict III observes that people readily recognise their good actions but struggle to notice their own wrongdoing. Anger, pride, cruelty, and jealousy obstruct that recognition. Ashoka’s ethical message therefore asked for self-examination as well as obedience: changing conduct required more than pointing to another person’s failings. [1]

chapters.title: An older ruler reviews his work
chapters.html: In his twenty-seventh year, Pillar Edict VII reviewed the problem of moral progress. Ashoka listed officers, instruction, donations, public works, and rules among his efforts. This is a king selecting what he wants remembered. It reveals his intentions and claims, but does not independently measure how every subject experienced his rule. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict VII: A royal review of dhamma

chapters.date: Twenty-seventh year · A judgment about change
chapters.title: Persuasion mattered more than rules alone
chapters.html: In that late review, Ashoka gave greater weight to persuasion than to regulation in changing conduct. A prohibition could restrain an act without producing understanding. The thought connects his practical rules with a larger ambition: people should learn to regard care and restraint as worthwhile, rather than act only from fear of punishment. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict VII: A royal review of dhamma

chapters.date: Later reign · Looking beyond his lifetime
chapters.title: He asked descendants to continue
chapters.html: Ashoka repeatedly looked beyond his own lifetime, addressing sons, grandsons, and later descendants. Durable inscriptions could preserve instructions, but could not guarantee future rulers’ priorities. His late appeals reveal both the ambition of the programme and its vulnerability: a personal royal commitment still depended on successors and officials to carry it forward. [1]

articles.title: Major Pillar Edict VII: A royal review of dhamma

chapters.date: c. 232 BCE · The end of the reign
chapters.title: Death around 232 BCE
chapters.html: Ashoka’s death is conventionally placed around 232 BCE. No surviving contemporary account describes his last illness, conversation, or funeral. Later Buddhist traditions give memorable endings, including the story of a diminished final gift. Such narratives teach about generosity and impermanence; their details are not verified deathbed records. [1, 6, 7]

chapters.date: After c. 232 BCE · Successors and Buddhist memory
chapters.title: The Mauryas continued after him
chapters.html: The empire did not disappear at Ashoka’s death. Inscriptions record Dasaratha’s later cave gifts to Ajivikas at Nagarjuni. Mauryan rule ended conventionally around 185 BCE, decades later. Explaining that decline simply as a result of Ashoka’s Buddhism goes beyond the evidence for institutions, resources, regional power, and the actions of successors. [1, 7]

chapters.title: A remembered king, sometimes troubling
chapters.html: Later literature contrasted cruel Chandashoka with righteous Dharmashoka. It also preserved stories of religious violence, miracles, and 84,000 stupas. These deserve scrutiny as later narratives, not automatic acceptance or silence. The stupa number is not an archaeological count, and allegations of persecution are not contemporary records from his reign. [7]

chapters.title: His inscriptions became readable again
chapters.html: James Prinsep’s work in 1837 was pivotal to deciphering Brahmi. Comparison with Pali chronicles, associated with George Turnour, helped identify Piyadasi with Ashoka. Later finds such as the Maski inscription supplied the personal name. Historical reconstruction joined the stones with knowledge that Buddhist communities had preserved over centuries. [1, 11]

articles.title: How Ashoka's Pillar Came to Tughlaq's Delhi: Forty-Two Wheels, One Ancient Mystery

chapters.title: His symbols entered modern India
chapters.html: Independent India adopted the Ashoka Chakra on its flag in 1947 and an adaptation of the Sarnath Lion Capital as its state emblem on 26 January 1950. “Satyameva Jayate” comes from the Mundaka Upanishad, not his edicts. Ancient imagery acquired new meaning within a republic, long after the emperor’s life. [12]

ashoka.sourcesHtml:
1. Ashoka’s contemporary inscriptions, in E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (1925), Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, volume I. The chief primary source for this account. Specific records discussed are Major Rock Edicts I–III, V–VI, VIII–IX, XI–XIV; the Separate Kalinga Edicts; Minor Rock Edict I; the Bairat and Schism Edicts; Pillar Edicts III–V and VII; the Queen’s Edict; the Lumbini and Nigali Sagar records; and the Barabar cave dedications. Regnal years and quantities above follow the particular inscriptions, with reported totals distinguished from independently verified counts. University of Oslo, Ashoka Library, for the inscription texts and Hultzsch’s English translations. Damaged readings, animal identifications, and terms for officials or fiscal arrangements can remain disputed.
  2. The Mahavamsa, translated by Wilhelm Geiger, chapter V, “The Third Council,” in The Mahavamsa, or The Great Chronicle of Ceylon (1912). Later Sri Lankan Buddhist tradition concerning the dynasty, succession, Nigrodha, religious patronage, and the council. It was compiled centuries after Ashoka and is not a contemporary palace record.
  3. The Mahavamsa, chapter XIII, “The Coming of Mahinda”, Geiger translation: Avanti, Ujjain, Vidisha, Devi, Mahinda, Sanghamitta, and the journey through the mother’s region. The family relationships and itinerary are attributed to this later chronicle.
  4. The Mahavamsa, chapters XII–XIV, in Geiger’s complete translation: missions, Mahinda’s journey, and the encounter with Devanampiyatissa. Compare the earlier Sri Lankan Dipavamsa, chapter VII, translated by Hermann Oldenberg, for traditions of the council and the ordination of Ashoka’s children. Neither text is a contemporary transcript of the events it narrates.
  5. The Mahavamsa, chapter XVIII, “The Receiving of the Great Bodhi-Tree”, and chapter XIX in Geiger’s complete translation: the request for Sanghamitta, the tree branch, the crossing, and the religious establishment in Lanka. Miracles and speeches belong to the chronicle’s religious narrative.
  6. The Mahavamsa, chapter XX, “The Nibbana of the Thera”, Geiger translation: Asandhamitta, Tissarakkha, the Bodhi tree, and the traditional chronology of the later reign. Its character judgments and motives are the chronicler’s.
  7. Northern Buddhist legends and their interpretation. Vincent A. Smith, Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, chapter VII, “The Indian Legends of Asoka”, public-domain collection and discussion of the Ashokavadana and related traditions: Taxila, succession, the torture-house, pilgrimage, Kunala, religious violence, and the final gift. Smith is a modern compiler, and his colonial-era interpretations are not adopted automatically. For the Sanskrit work and its religious setting, John S. Strong, The Legend of King Asoka: A Study and Translation of the Asokavadana, originally published in the 1980s. The Ashokavadana tradition took written form long after Ashoka’s lifetime; its episodes are identified as later testimony throughout this account.
  8. Kandahar texts. The Greek inscriptions of Ashoka at Kandahar, with the editions and translation sources identified there; the bilingual Greek-Aramaic record and the separate Greek text are distinct inscriptions. Francesco Maniscalco, “A New Interpretation of the Edicts of Aśoka from Kandahar”, Annali di Ca’ Foscari. Serie orientale 54 (2018), pp. 239–263, for the regional and linguistic setting and interpretive problems. This modern study is distinct from the original inscriptional evidence.
  9. National Museum, New Delhi, “Rock edict: Edict of Ashoka”, the museum’s account of its cast of the Girnar edicts. Its summaries provide an accessible institutional introduction; the full source texts in reference 1 are used for detailed claims.
  10. Sanchi’s successive building phases. UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi”, for the long development of the complex. The later gateways and reliefs are distinguished from the earliest Mauryan patronage and from contemporary portraits.
  11. The inscriptions’ later history. James Prinsep’s 1837 Brahmi studies and the identification with the Pali chronicles are discussed alongside the primary publications in the Sources of the internal article The Ashokan Pillar at Topra and Firuz Shah’s Delhi. Its archaeological and historical references also document the pillar’s fourteenth-century movement. The decipherment and the continued preservation of Buddhist historical memory are distinct parts of the reconstruction.
  12. Government of India, official national-symbols booklet, and “National Emblem,” Presentation Gov, and the Constituent Assembly flag resolution of 22 July 1947: the modern adoption of the emblem, the Ashoka Chakra, and the origin of Satyameva Jayate. These sources concern the modern use of ancient imagery, not the intentions of Ashoka’s court.
